column2: Elaine de Kooning publishes in Art News (November 1950, pp. 40-43, 57-58) an article on Josef Albers, the former Bauhaus master then teaching at Yale, whom she had known at Black Mountain. Art News, November 1950, pages 40-43 and 57-58. Consequences: The article is reprinted in her collected writings; it documents her view of Albers's teaching.

Richards stages her translation of Cocteau's Marriage on the Eiffel Tower; the dining hall becomes a total environment, with the platform of the Eiffel Tower towering over a Paris skyline; actors and audience eat Thanksgiving dinner there before the play. Atmosphere: Paris re-created in the mountains of North Carolina Stakes: the fusion of the community meal and total theater

After the meal, served on a set representing a terrace of the Eiffel Tower, Cocteau's play begins: the photographer (June Rice Christensen, in a checked jacket and a puffed-up wig, on a ladder behind the shutter of the giant camera) tries to photograph the wedding party; an ostrich bursts out of the camera, a hunter chases it through the latticework, a lion devours a guest, a cyclist asks the way to Chatou, telegrams fall from the sky, a General tells about his wasp pie; finally the bride and groom and all their guests vanish into the camera, and the camera leaves the stage trailing its bellows like a wagon. Hazel Larsen Archer, in the audience, takes photographs: through the openings in the bellows one sees the guests waving handkerchiefs, and feet walking. Words: The set represented the first-level terrace of the Eiffel Tower; the bellows follows the camera “like a wagon”. Atmosphere: Absurd, slapstick, carnivalesque: joyful chaos in the blurred light of motion that Archer captures. Stakes: A camera that devours its subjects, photographed by a camera in dialogue with them: the scene grounds the argument of the whole study of Archer.

The disintegration of Levi's marriage over the following six months drives him out of the community in December 1950; Corkran decides to leave in the fall of 1950, he, Trayer, the Quakers, and Goldowski giving up on any responsible reorganization. Consequences: Consolidation of the “new” Black Mountain
Levi leaves the community; Richards decides to stay, making their separation final. Consequences: Richards then plays a decisive part in the 1951 recruiting

His mother, who after his father threw him out had searched blindly through the streets of Philadelphia, writes to ask whether he is coming home for Christmas; Rumaker refuses, writing a lie; he wants neither to leave Merrill nor to face his family, and wants to be there when Olson returns soon Hundreds of miles hitchhiking to his parents' home, then the trip back

For the holidays, their neighbor Cissy Oppenheimer gives each of them an orange studded with cloves; the couple breathe them in under the quilt during the first heavy snows (mostly melted by noon the next day in this quickly softening climate) Fragrant clove-studded oranges, heavy snow melting at noon, the bare trees of the Seven Sisters smoking in the crisp air
Letters written to Robert Creeley, who edits them and publishes them in 1953 in Palma, Majorca (Divers Press). Epigraph of The Maximus Poems: “All my life I've heard / one makes many”

Elaine is listed as a dependent on Bill's 1951 tax return. Bill's income: $7,610, including $4,000 for the first prize of the Art Institute of Chicago for Excavation (1950); $1,750 in medical expenses for Elaine's broken leg; the Sidney Janis Gallery advances him money for supplies. Income $7,610; prize $4,000; medical expenses $1,750 Consequences: Sales gradually improve over the decade

Dord Fitz, an artist, teacher, and dealer in Amarillo, Texas, is arrested on a “morals charge” after a homosexual encounter and fired from the University of Kentucky; he will remain a man with a family secret. Dismissal from the University of Kentucky Consequences: Fitz now wears a masked self, a secret he fears a portrait by Elaine might reveal
Williams meets Lou Harrison again, whom he had glimpsed at Town Hall in 1949, and becomes his friend during the summer at the college. Consequences: A lasting friendship between the two men.

When Williams drives to Asheville to the ABC store (the state liquor store), Harrison asks him for a bottle of Rock and Rye. Rock and Rye: a rye whiskey liqueur flavored with rock-candy syrup and fruit, repulsively sweet; the only person Williams knew who liked it; the product has disappeared from ABC stores.

Tudor comes as accompanist to the dancer Katherine Litz; concerts of works by Webern, Schoenberg, Cage, Lou Harrison, Stefan Wolpe, and student composers. He prepares the New York premiere of Boulez's Second Sonata for the fall; Richards goes with him to New York and translates Artaud there, setting the stage for Cage's first happening, performed at the college. Concert program, the Boulez premiere in New York Consequences: Translation of The Theater and Its Double, the atmosphere of the happening

Mildred and Branwen explore the site by looking through windows and find an enormous rusty kerosene stove; the driver of the college's old pickup helps bring it down to their kitchen A rusty kerosene stove; only a kettle brought along, no pots and pans and no food Consequences: A step out of the stone age; tea and coffee now possible

In a tutorial, after reading his stories (about grown men, including a middle-aged alcoholic actor seeking salvation in a Bowery church), Olson thundered that they were pure shit and ordered him to keep nothing but a journal, an hour a day at least, and to come back the next summer to show it to him. A journal for at least an hour a day, for a year Consequences: Gray obeyed, kept his journal throughout his senior year, changed his thesis to “Kierkegaard's View on the Demise of Christianity,” and came back in the summer of 1952, on the threshold of his vocation as a writer

The witness's first summer: supercool poses of silence; bare feet, long hair, and dark glasses on the men; easy nudism and bisexuality: fads of the nascent Beat Generation, forerunners of the style of the 1960s. She cuts her hair short and ragged, like a punk. Hair cut very short and uneven; widespread imitation of Olson's phonetic spellings (waz, enuf, luv, kulchur, yrself, ga-wan, Ru-man-tick, egg-zack-tly), borrowed secondhand from the Pound of the 1920s

A young woman dances in front of the mirror in the main hall from 7 a.m. until dinner, stopping only to feed the baby squalling in a basket by the exercise barre. She takes no classes and speaks to no one: ten hours on end watching herself in the mirror. 7 a.m. to dinner, about ten hours; basket; exercise barre; mirror

At dinner, Olson, bare-chested under a serape thrown over his shoulders, sits next to Cage, always very formal in a black city suit, tie, and very shiny pointed black shoes; Cage punctuates the table's cultivated terseness with his Zen-monk laugh while pondering his next Happening. Serape; black suit; crystalline laugh; pointed patent-leather shoes

She goes with the poet Jonathan Williams to the draft board when he refuses induction into the US Army as a conscientious objector. Consequences: She sees in it a political education as important as the one she received from her family or her college

Rauschenberg helps the author of the account unload his old '39 Ford; he discovers a bundle of small canvases that the author meant to reuse, covered with zinc white through which the original compositions could be made out; Rauschenberg is enthusiastic about these whited-out canvases. An old 1939 Ford; small canvases covered with a coat of zinc white; the original shapes faintly visible underneath Consequences: The author, disconcerted, feels less sure of what he will paint on these canvases

A few days after his arrival, the author sees Twombly sitting on the steps of South Lodge, helping Rauschenberg apply flat white paint to a series of stretched canvases, the very ones that will become the White Paintings. Flat white paint brushed onto stretched canvases, on the steps Consequences: These canvases will be shown at the Betty Parsons Gallery
In early 1951, the college sends out a few inquiries to attract Black students; the only result is a stern rebuke from a Black educator for writing “Negro” with a lowercase n.

Rumors filter back to Black Mountain: some members are not doing their share, finances are unstable, the mechanics of daily life leave little time for interpersonal exploration. The community dissolves after three years, an orderly dissolution, Wallen stresses, not a breakup in discord. The members, about fifty with children and grandchildren scattered along the Pacific Coast, still gather every Thanksgiving for five days. Three years; ~50 people; an annual five-day reunion at Thanksgiving Consequences: Secret satisfaction among some at Black Mountain
In the early 1950s, when Cage takes the path of chance and “indeterminacy,” Albers tells him that he has abdicated his responsibility as an artist; their sympathy and friendship are broken.
The marriage, known to be fragile, ends in a separation in 1951.

In the spring of 1951, after a new round of factionalism, a very different Black Mountain emerges, almost the opposite of what Natasha, the Quakers, Pittenger, Trayer, and Corkran had worked to build; all of them leave the college in disgust, for different reasons and at different times; Duberman notes how murky the alignments are: each principal participant assures him that all his other sources are inaccurate Natasha and Bill Levi, fountainheads of the conflict, their personalities often counting for more than questions of educational policy Consequences: Natasha goes from being a discreet member on the periphery (before 1948-49) to the real leader in power after the departure of the Alberses and the Dreiers

Olson proposes to title this period “The Afterwards, or the Original Damsel Re'deemed,” from 1951 on, with no end date. For him, Black Mountain returns to the core of the old apple: what Rice said in the first catalog, that the arts share the center of the curriculum with ordinary studies. Like Rice, Olson believes in renting, in not becoming an “institution”: having inherited an institution, he dismantles it and sells it off piece by piece so that something else can live: the people, the life in them. Title proposed by Olson: “The Afterwards, or the Original Damsel Re'deemed — you might call 1951 on — with no end date known or in sight!” Consequences: A radical individualization of the experience, the “chief glory of Black Mountain” according to Duberman

More or less amicable departures: the Jennerjahns leave to finish Pete's GI Bill with a year in France; Turner opens a full-time pottery in New York State; the Trayers leave to farm at Earlham; Paul Leser joins Hartford Seminary for the salary; Natasha leaves for a year in Paris, less graciously. Consequences: Several vacancies to fill
Out of many candidates, only Victor Sprague (biology) and John Adams (anthropology) receive and accept an offer. Consequences: A much reduced resident faculty

Olson returns to stay, straight from Lerma (Yucatán), with his collection y & x. Richards, away for the summer, offers him her apartment and her place for “room and board”; Fitton and Oppenheimer collect a hundred dollars among the students as a token salary, and that is enough to persuade him. $100 collected among the students Consequences: Olson becomes the heart of the college for its last five years
Ed Dorn prints Olson's text on the college press; Olson describes it as an attack not on the university but on the universe.

During the summer of 1951, Tudor plays Boulez's Second Sonata; Olson declares something to the effect that it is the only piece of music since Bach. Consequences: Williams comments that Olson had heard only three pieces since Bach, but liked people who said outrageous things.

Williams writes “cummings/Patchen” pastiches full of fog and golden singing snakes; Olson, who likes neither Patchen nor cummings and is very heavy with him, tears them apart with a “vast owlish distaste”; it takes about two months for them to become friends. “fog and gold singing snakes”; “vast owlish distaste” Consequences: An initial falling-out, then friendship

First issue in the spring of 1951; the magazine becomes the meeting place of many writers who will later appear in The Black Mountain Review and be called the “Black Mountain School of Poets.” Consequences: A forerunner of The Black Mountain Review

Origin publishes its first issue in the spring of 1951; it becomes the meeting place of many future contributors to The Black Mountain Review, later called the “Black Mountain School of Poets.” Consequences: Prepares the ground for the 1954 magazine.
For his photograph in the BMC catalog for fall 1951, Olson chooses the motto “For use, now”. BMC catalog, fall 1951

Shahn, who taught painting there the previous summer, praises the unconventional virtues of Black Mountain College and is enthusiastic about Charles Olson, the giant poet who teaches writing there. Consequences: Rumaker writes to the college; this is the origin of the whole story

Asked about Black Mountain, the painter Mary Reed says she has heard of it as a nest of communists and homosexuals, which, at the height of the McCarthy era, makes it all the more attractive to Rumaker. Consequences: Strengthens his decision to go

Connie mentions Rauschenberg, a painting student who left in the spring, whose “Black on Black” and then “White on White” caused a stir in New York avant-garde circles. Consequences: The college's influence beyond its walls.

Purchase of Origin No. 2 (summer 1951) from Carroll Williams; the poem “A Po-sy, A Po-sy” leaves him utterly baffled (“aw, piss, and sing, be / robert burns...”), to the point of doubting his intuition. A thin magazine bought at the college store Consequences: Doubts about Olson, quickly dispelled by his personal magnetism

After Olson's return, as Olson urges them to read Dostoevsky, Rumaker devours the novels in the library and adapts the Grand Inquisitor chapter into a one-act play for Wes's class: a Spanish prison cell at night, two characters, Christ at his Second Coming threatening the benevolent tyranny of the Church; a pure transcription with no dramaturgy; Wes reads the whole “adaptation” aloud in class, and he and Duck Daley respond with compassionate tolerance Consequences: A failed apprenticeship; Rumaker is too naive to see its shortcomings

Two years earlier, Rumaker tells his mother that he will no longer go to church; she shouts at him to go see a psychiatrist, he at her to stop the blackmail; after their only explosive fight, she huddles silently by the window. His father then throws him out. The priest advises her that it is only a phase and that he will come back to the fold. He walks past the parlor to catch the bus to his factory job without another word; information received later from a sister-in-law. Consequences: The first separation; the second is BMC itself.

Rumaker discovers Creeley's writing in the summer 1951 issue of Origin, a magazine edited by Cid Corman in Boston, devoted to Creeley. Stories “In the Summer,” “3 Fate Tales,” “Mr. Blue”; poems “Love” and “Hart Crane (2)”; most of the texts unpublished elsewhere, even by Divers Press Consequences: The beginning of a lasting fascination

In the fall of 1951, before Rosenberg's article on Action Painting, Elaine describes Smith's way of working and draws an aesthetic from it: the artist's moral integrity comes from his honest collaboration with materials and his will to find, not repeat, an image; the finished work is the sum of the gestures made in the material. An industrial workshop: concrete floors, north skylights, a potbellied stove, tools powered by a Ford engine; a radio playing classical music; work clothes Consequences: She establishes the critical approach others will use and sketches the archetype of the American artist as existentialist hero; in the eyes of the Club she becomes a star-maker

Coming from New Jersey, Hartigan sees Pollock's first drip paintings; the experience changes her life. She remembers being “bowled over, really confused and moved in an extraordinary way”. Consequences: She decides to learn from Pollock.

Pollock gets brutally drunk, shouts obscenities, comes close to violence; Lee reasons with him like a child until he sinks into an alcoholic stupor, then sells Pollock to Hartigan as a genius. Sober, Pollock is almost mute; drunk, he talks about art and declares: “There are only two guys in town… Pollock and de Kooning”. Pollock recommends going to see de Kooning's second show at Charles Egan's and telling Bill that he sent her. Consequences: Hartigan goes to the Egan Gallery, then to de Kooning's studio.

Large black enamel drawings: Hartigan finds them magnificent, kin to Pollock in energy, rebellion, gesture, and power. Large black enamel drawings (“black enamel drawings”). Consequences: She immediately goes to visit de Kooning.

Hartigan knocks downstairs; Bill sticks his head out the window with his Dutch accent (“Who's dat?” “Come on up, den”); she finds him compact, magnificent, a movie star. Elaine bursts in, flirts ostentatiously with Bill, and asks him for money for a winter coat, having already spent the sum he gave her. Hartigan dislikes her at first, then judges her intelligent and serious about one thing: Bill's genius. Bill says of Jackson: “Yah, Jackson is something”; a quarrel over money for a winter coat. Consequences: Hartigan becomes a witness to the couple and to the Pollock-de Kooning rivalry.

A group of artists encouraged by Leo Castelli takes over a vast vacant commercial space; the exhibition, extended at the Stable Gallery, publicly defines the core of Abstract Expressionism. Consequences: Those left out become second-rank figures.
Bill shows large black enamel drawings and vivid abstract paintings; praise from the critics but very few sales. Consequences: His reputation grows nonetheless, despite the lack of collectors.

Bill takes part in the MoMA symposium connected with the exhibition Abstract Painting and Sculpture in America; his statement is published in the 1951 MoMA Bulletin. Consequences: His ideas on art reach a wide audience

Publication of the book that grew out of an initial manuscript by Perls, developed by Goodman (volume II) and put into practice by Hefferline (volume I); the three declare themselves equally responsible, having resolved their differences by confronting them rather than politely hiding them. Copyright 1951; Library of Congress card 51-14876; Dell Publishing, 750 Third Avenue, New York 17; cover by David Passalaqua; marked “Nineteenth Printing” Consequences: The book becomes the founding text of Gestalt therapy.

Publication of the book containing the chapter on retroflection, with experiments meant to be practiced by readers and students. Experiment No. 13: “Mobilizing the Muscles” Consequences: The text becomes a source of theory and exercises for possible workshops.
She makes her first poem-drawings while waiting for the birth of her son Consequences: The start of her work combining words and images

Chaet, who has come from Boston for the interview, is told by Albers to bring the canvases rather than slides; Albers critiques her work, asks how she would teach, and hires her on the spot, without a committee, in an hour and a half. An interview of about 1 hour 30 minutes; Chaet and Robert Scott are Albers's only outside hires Consequences: Chaet joins the department; admissions follow the same model
Albers presents an untitled text at the International Design Conference during the summer of 1951. JAAF archives.
A 1951 summer session centered on a single medium, photography, bringing together Harry Callahan, Arthur Siegel, and Aaron Siskind. Consequences: Inspires the Pottery Seminar of fall 1952

Larsen organizes a summer session devoted to photography and invites Callahan, Siskind, and Siegel, then on their way to becoming major figures in the history of photography. Callahan and Siegel were then teaching at the Institute of Design in Chicago; Siskind will join its faculty the following year. Consequences: Creative photography as a subject of study was then in its infancy in the United States

Williams, turned down for Callahan's class at the Institute of Design in Chicago, follows Callahan's advice to enroll at Black Mountain; there he falls under the spell of Charles Olson, and his interest shifts from photography to writing and publishing. Consequences: Founding (just before his arrival, in a Chinese restaurant in San Francisco with David Ruffin) of the Jargon Society, a small press that became a project of the BMC Museum

Oates, a devoted student of Larsen's, becomes the college's first graduate in photography; his work is evaluated by the outside examiner Edward Steichen, director of the photography department at MoMA.
Appointed music director; there he composes, among other works, “Gamelan” (Suite for Violin, Piano, and Small Orchestra, 1952) and the music for Glyph (1951).

A multimedia work: Harrison's music for an eccentric amateur ensemble (piano, bells, claves, plus optional gong and tuning fork), choreography by Katherine Litz, who struggles inside a body sock, a curtain painted by Ben Shahn inspired by Maya glyphs and Chinese calligraphy, and Olson's poetry on race, slavery, and community in the modern South. Piano, bells, claves, gong, tuning fork, body sock
Photograph of Katherine Litz dancing The Glyph at the college Photograph held in the Jerome Robbins Dance Division, New York Public Library for the Performing Arts

In the spring of 1951, Turner resigns for family reasons and for lack of predictable time in the pot shop. He had not grasped BMC's experimental ethos while there, but will later say that the college's artistic philosophy affected his perception in the years that followed. Consequences: Search for a successor.

Karnes and Weinrib spend a working year in Sesto Fiorentino; Karnes meets the industrialist-architect Gio Ponti there and produces Double Vase, published in Domus and then awarded a prize at the Sixteenth Ceramic Annual of the Everson Museum in Syracuse.

To keep the college solvent, Richards restructures the program with year-round thematic institutes and renowned guest artists on two-month contracts. Flyer for the Summer Session in the Arts, July 9 to August 31, 1951; letter to the faculty: about four guest artists on two-month contracts nourishing the whole year, a pedagogy of abundance
Jonathan Williams publishes The Dancer under the Jargon Press name, pairing a poem by Oppenheimer with an ink drawing by Rauschenberg, commemorating a dance by Katherine Litz in New York.
Siegel teaches a two-week workshop during the summer of 1951; his own practice is then mostly devoted to color photography. Two weeks.

Siskind, resistant to the strict, design-centered Bauhaus pedagogy, finds at BMC an open, experimental approach in which feeling and expression are encouraged; he photographs in North Carolina and Kentucky (North Carolina 11). Themes: torn posters, water-damaged surfaces, scrawled letters. Consequences: He accepts the post at the ID for the fall of 1951.

On his return, Albers is gone and the atmosphere has shifted from intensive coursework to individual experiment. Rauschenberg arrives with Twombly, whom he had met at the Art Students League in New York. Anecdote: a jealous student tells Jack Tworkov he does not understand why he spends so much time with Bob, who never goes to class; Tworkov replies that he takes an interest in students once they stop going to class. Twombly was then painting highly gestural black-and-white abstract canvases close to the biomorphic and the vegetal Consequences: Beginning of the Black Paintings

Olson spends five months in Lerma, Mexico, studying the remains of Maya culture; he brings back a renewed relationship to the letter, both as an epistolary unit and as a concrete form. Five months Consequences: His art renewed around the glyph; an echo of the Alberses' stay in Mexico

Shahn draws a design for a dance performance directly on the body of the student Nicholas Cernovich; the design serves as the basis for “A Glyph for Charles” and for two large drawings, Down Fall and Nicolas C (1951). Two large derived drawings: Down Fall and Nicolas C

Harrison composes The Glyph for prepared piano, two bells, claves, a pitchfork, and perhaps a gong; six movements ranging from standard notation to instructions for improvisation. Scores in ink on music paper, 8½ × 11 inches each; the instruction “follow dance” scattered through the score Consequences: The musical side of the exchange

A nine-minute solo: Litz appears and disappears six times behind a 4 × 8-foot panel painted with an enlarged version of Shahn's drawing, turning a jersey tube costume into a succession of characters (mermaid → tree → stone sculpture → animal). Nine minutes; a 4 × 8-foot panel; a jersey tube costume; the panel painted by Charles Oscar, then Litz's husband; David Tudor accompanied Litz as pianist
Lecture on realism given during the 1951 summer session; transcript preserved.

In 1951, Archer organizes a summer institute devoted to photography, inviting Aaron Siskind, Arthur Siegel, and Harry Callahan as guest lecturers, and mounts photography exhibitions on campus. Consequences: The high point of photography at BMC under Archer's influence.

Archer organizes a summer institute devoted to photography, invites Siskind, Siegel, and Callahan as guest lecturers, and mounts photography exhibitions on campus Consequences: Students are exposed to the history of photography and to a range of styles

Rauschenberg paints large canvases in oil, then presses them directly into the North Carolina earth by moonlight Consequences: A series Molesworth reads as an abandonment of authorship, close to indexical photography

Archer invites two teachers from the Institute of Design in Chicago to teach at BMC during the summer of 1951, establishing institutional ties between BMC and the offspring of the Bauhaus in the United States. Consequences: A rapprochement between BMC and the New Bauhaus/Institute of Design through photography

Asawa's wire objects are shown with Calder mobiles; Ray Johnson, a friend from BMC, describes a hanging piece as enclosing “forms within forms within forms”. Her most complex piece to date: Untitled (S.535), 2.20 m (about 7 feet) high, five lobes, photographed by Cunningham for the cover of Arts and Architecture and in Domus Consequences: Asawa's first major visibility

An eight-foot copper sculpture, hanging from the ceiling and weighing twenty pounds, first accepted and then rejected: the jurors doubted it was sculpture. “It wasn't stone, it wasn't welded steel… They thought it was craft, or something else, but not art,” Asawa would say Consequences: Illustrates the exclusion of domestically coded mediums from the realm of fine art

Asawa is working on a folded-paper wall covering, the very one later shown at the Laverne showroom in San Francisco; Renk finds in it the solution to the unsolved problem from his design school. Wall covering; Laverne showroom. Consequences: Sets off the passing on of folding to Renk.

After the exercises explained by Asawa (derived from Albers), Renk learns the rules of folding, then spends two days and two nights designing and folding a shape like an egg carton. Two days and two nights of work. Consequences: A series of folded pendants, including Folded (1953).
Published by the Black Mountain Graphics Workshop in 1951.
Takes part in the annual exhibition with two White Paintings.
Spends the end of the summer and the fall at the college. Consequences: Collaboration with Cage, illustration for Jargon Press
Makes the print Automobile Tire Print with Cage.
Illustrates Joel Oppenheimer's poem “The Dancer,” published at Black Mountain College by Jonathan Williams as the second publication in the Jargon Press series.
Rauschenberg takes part in the annual exhibition and shows two “White Paintings” there. Two White Paintings
After the publicity in Life, Sue and Bob ask their friends Liberman and Brodovitch for work: many tantalizing promises, no jobs.
Rauschenberg spends the end of the summer and the fall at the college.
Rauschenberg and Cage make the automobile tire print together.
Rauschenberg illustrates the poem published at the college by Jonathan Williams, the second publication in the Jargon Press series. Second Jargon Press title

A monotype made with John Cage: sheets of paper glued into a long strip are laid out on the pavement of Fulton Street; Rauschenberg inks a section of the street, and Cage drives his Model A Ford through the ink and then onto the paper. According to Rauschenberg's account in an interview, Cage was the only one who owned a car and was willing to take part; he simply had to stay on the paper, and he did an excellent job. English version of the catalog: twenty glued sheets; German interview version: fifty pieces, a print six meters long; Model A Ford; Cage the only driver Consequences: With the blueprints, the only work to lay the foundations of what followed: the direct trace of the object on the support, the role of chance in an organized action

Rauschenberg paints the series of white monochromes in ordinary house paint applied with a roller on identical canvas panels assembled as a triptych. He knows from the start that they will have to be repainted when the color yellows; he writes to Betty Parsons in October 1951 to say that the maker of these paintings is today. Ordinary house paint, roller, identical panels; letter to Betty Parsons, October 1951; repainted later with the help of Brice Marden Consequences: The white canvases will be reused for other works when canvas runs short, for example Trophy II
A group of portraits of Susan Weil, Rauschenberg's wife, pregnant with their son Christopher, posing and lying down in Central Park

Betty Parsons comes to select the paintings, accompanied by Clyfford Still, who says almost nothing and takes no part in the choice; Rauschenberg cannot keep from reworking much of the selection to improve it. Apartment on West 96th Street; Still's silence

Beginning of a friendship based on mutual admiration and sympathy; it strengthens Rauschenberg's anti-expressionist attitude. Consequences: A conscious elimination of symbolism, depth, and expression from his art
The curators cite the White Paintings (1951), painted just after his time at Black Mountain, as the iconoclastic origin of the minimalist sensibility the exhibition examines.

Rauschenberg makes entirely white multipanel paintings that reject the heroism of Abstract Expressionism; their blank surfaces are designed to record the shadows of viewers and the temporality of the viewing experience Multipanel paintings, bare white surfaces Consequences: They influence a generation of sculptors and painters and directly inspire John Cage's 4'33''
